speaker: Tobias Lütke
title: Tobi Lütke: 21 Years of Building Shopify
question: In technology startups, why can building outside a dominant industry hub like Silicon Valley produce stronger differentiation?
guest: I think inside Silicon Valley there's just too much cross-pollination. Entropy creates equilibria, so you end up with companies being very recognizably similar to each other. The activation energy for being very different is super high because people move between companies, come with the wrong ideas into your company, behave incorrectly, and you have to tell them to behave differently. Early on I traveled to Silicon Valley a few times a year to learn as much as I could. But of course what I got from everyone was not actually the answers to how to do things—I was getting their aspirations or the highlight reel, the best version of what their company ought to be doing. I took those ideas back home, localized them to our problems, and tried to do something better. Only many years later did I realize I was always comparing our real average to everyone else's aspirations and highlight reel—and trying to beat that actually makes you do much better.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Building outside a dominant hub can strengthen differentiation mainly because distance breaks you out of the hub's shared thinking. In a place like Silicon Valley, founders, investors, and engineers circulate among the same companies, read the same things, and chase the same fashionable ideas, which pushes startups toward similar products, business models, and target customers. Outside that echo chamber, founders are more likely to form independent views and notice problems the hub overlooks.

Proximity to different customers and industries matters too. A startup in a manufacturing, agriculture, energy, logistics, or healthcare centre sees real-world problems firsthand and can build domain expertise and customer relationships that hub-based competitors struggle to replicate.

Scarcer capital also shapes companies differently. With less venture funding available, startups tend to focus earlier on revenue, capital efficiency, and sustainable unit economics rather than growth at all costs.

Finally, talent dynamics help: lower costs extend runway, and employees face fewer poaching offers, so teams stay together longer and accumulate deeper institutional knowledge.

The trade-off is real, though: thinner networks, fewer experienced operators, and harder fundraising.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Building outside a dominant hub like Silicon Valley insulates startups from the monoculture and consensus thinking that push founders toward the same fashionable problems, business models, and technical playbooks. In dense ecosystems, shared investor networks, social circles, and rapid employee turnover create strong mimetic pressure, often leading startups to build for other tech companies and optimize for whatever metrics local venture capitalists currently reward.

Geographic distance breaks that echo chamber. Founders outside major hubs often sit closer to traditional industries—such as manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, healthcare, or regional commerce—giving them firsthand insight into unglamorous, high-value problems that hub insiders overlook. Less access to easy venture capital, paired with lower operating costs, can also enforce strategic discipline, steering teams toward customer-funded growth, durable unit economics, and unconventional distribution rather than hype-driven blitzscaling. Finally, less poaching and job-hopping help startups retain employees longer, allowing teams to compound idiosyncratic domain expertise and a distinct organizational culture instead of recycling standardized industry orthodoxy.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Building away from a dominant hub can produce stronger differentiation mainly because it weakens herd effects. In Silicon Valley, founders draw on the same investors, advisors, talent pools, and conversations, so their ideas, business models, and even pitch decks tend to look alike. Firms chase whatever theses are fashionable and end up competing in crowded categories.

Founders elsewhere are exposed to different problems, customers, and industries, such as agriculture in the Midwest, logistics in Memphis, or energy in Houston. That gives them access to knowledge that is local and hard to copy, and to unmet needs that hub-based teams overlook or misread. Paul Graham and Peter Thiel's "contrarian truth" idea both suggest that the best opportunities lie where consensus isn't looking.

Cost and competition also matter. Cheaper talent and rent extend a startup's runway, so it can be patient. Less fierce competition for engineers means better retention and less copying of tactics. With fewer nearby rivals, a company can build a defensible niche before others notice.

The trade-off is thinner access to capital, experienced operators, and networks. Remote work and distributed venture funding have reduced, but not eliminated, those disadvantages.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Building outside a dominant hub like Silicon Valley insulates a startup from the intense groupthink that often drives founders in major tech centers toward the same fashionable markets, business models, and technical architectures. When founders are not immersed in a tight echo chamber of investors and peers chasing identical trends, they are more likely to develop independent convictions and contrarian product designs.

Geographic distance also exposes teams to overlooked, real-world problems rooted in local industries—such as logistics, healthcare, manufacturing, or regional finance—that hub-based founders rarely experience firsthand. Solving those unglamorous, domain-specific pain points naturally yields defensible differentiation.

Finally, operating in a less saturated market changes how companies build. Lower competition for talent often produces lower attrition and deeper institutional knowledge, while scarcer venture capital encourages earlier focus on customer revenue and unit economics rather than consensus growth tactics. Together, these pressures reward originality over conformity.

Building outside a dominant tech hub can expose founders to customers, industries, and talent that startups inside the hub tend to overlook. Founders who spend time with local manufacturers, for example, may spot workflow problems that rarely come up in Silicon Valley investor meetings. Those relationships can help them test a product early and earn the trust of customers that competitors would struggle to reach.

Distance can also reduce the pressure to chase the same trends, hire from the same networks, and build for the same early adopters. Geography becomes an advantage when it gives a startup a better view of an underserved problem or access to people who can help solve it.
